lecons.html:
Is love a big word? It is. We never stop trying to define this word, despite everything the dictionary says about it. The Bible devotes an entire chapter to it (1 Cor 13). We say this because we are willing to let the first letter of John deal with another subject. Otherwise, we would say that his book is an apology for this virtue. It is also he who gives the weightiest sentence in the world: God is love (1 John 4:8). Or, if you prefer to say it the other way around, love is of God (1 John 4:7).

To love is to have an intense feeling of affection and attachment toward a being, so that one is driven to seek a physical, intellectual, spiritual or even imaginary closeness with that being.

The greatest commandment has only one object: love.

“Jesus answered, “The greatest is, ‘Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first commandment. The second is like this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.”” (Mark 12:29-31)

Love is the distinctive sign of the disciple of Jesus Christ. The Lord says: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”” (John 13:34-35)

The apostle John adds: “No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.” (1 John 4:12) “We know and have believed the love which God has for us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” (1 John 4:16)

But love must not be an empty word. We must live it in practice, as the apostle urges us: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth. And by this we know that we are of the truth, and persuade our hearts before him,” (1 John 3:18-19)

When we read the book of Acts, we see how the Christians of the early faith lived love. They had everything in common. They remembered one another in their prayers. They came to one another’s help without thinking of themselves first. These Christians could give to others out of their meager and insufficient resources. Because they lived like this, there were no needy people among them. When they gathered to pray, they prayed in agreement and received quick answers.

We must return to this model. The apostles’ letters insisted on the question of brotherly love so that everyone would keep in step. We must also keep insisting on the practice of love and find every means to free the Christian world from selfishness.

It must be said that at one point our fathers began to lose this love. That is why the head of the Church had to call them back to order: “But I have this against you, that you left your first love. Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works; or else I am coming to you swiftly, and will move your lamp stand out of its place, unless you repent.” (Rev 2:4-5)

We must also practice those first works. We must love God and our neighbor, each as is fitting. Before looking at the love we must give, however, it is good to think about the love that has already been given to us:

John 3:16, John 15:9, John 15:12-13, John 16:26-27, Rom 5:8, 1 John 3:1, 1 John 4:9-10, 1 John 4:19.

God loved us first. He has loved us since the foundation of the world. And God proved his love toward us by giving Jesus Christ so that we might be saved through him.

Jesus Christ expressly declared that the Father loves us, and that he himself loves us. That is why he gave himself for us. The Holy Spirit’s love for us is not proved by words. It is proved by the very fact that he came to dwell in us. The Holy Spirit is sensitive, he is holy and therefore cannot tolerate the presence of sin at all. But in order to keep us for himself, there was no other way than the presence of the Holy Spirit in us. Indeed, the Holy Spirit is the mark that identifies us with God, he is the guarantee of our resurrection and of our rapture (Rom 8:11, 2 Cor 1:22, Eph 1:13-14, 4:30).

What are the implications of God’s love for us?

For our present life and our future, this implies many wonderful things: 1 John 3:1-2, Eph 2:3-7, Eph 1:4-5, John 16:26-27, 2 Thess 2:16-17.

We are children of God now and enjoy the privileges attached to it, such as God’s close care for us (1 Pet 5:7). God brought us back from death in sins to life in his righteousness, and seated us in the heavenly places in Christ. We are in a position of strength. What we are is an irrevocable decision of God, founded in his love. And God is love. He cannot change his mind. Our life of holiness depends no more on our exercise of godliness than it depends on the love of God. It is quite the other way around. God loves us and, by virtue of that, has decided to have us holy and blameless before him. It is a duty he has imposed on himself and he will do everything to succeed in it. In God’s love we have the promise, the strength and all the resources necessary to live holy and blameless.

God’s love for us also implies that he answers our prayers. We do not need to play with words or formulas to catch his attention. God loves us so much that he listens to the slightest sighs of our hearts, pays attention to them in order to understand and act accordingly.

As for our future, in his love God gave us eternal comfort and good hope by his grace. The hope in question is the experience of God’s glory at the return of our Lord Jesus Christ. This is what serves as our eternal comfort in the difficulties of this walk with Christ. In his love, God will make sure that we are ready for the return of Jesus Christ. It is by virtue of God’s love that you, by the power of God, are kept through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time (1 Pet 1:5). This salvation is the transformation of our body into the likeness of that of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming. It is guaranteed. Believe it. God is not a loser who finds reasons to justify his failure.

Jesus said: “In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you. If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also.” (John 14:2-3)

It is a promise that he must keep. And he gave no conditions for coming and then making excuses. The only condition is faith in his love. That is why Jude wrote: “But you, beloved, keep building up yourselves on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves in God’s love, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to eternal life.” (Jude 1:20-21). If you keep faith in God’s love, you will be carried to live for him, to bring him your weaknesses in prayer, and so be made, by his power, able to walk in holiness. In this way, you cannot miss the rapture. It is simply impossible.

You know this verse: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Gal 2:20). In this declaration, the central word is faith, faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself up for me. By his love he gave himself for me, by his love he went to prepare a place for me, by his love he promised to come back and take me with him, and by his love he will keep his word. I believe it.

By his love, God covers us in every way. He covers our many sins, he covers our weaknesses, he covers our livelihood and he covers our future. We can count on him because he loves us.

God’s love gives us the platform to love and to enjoy love. We can love without fear of being taken advantage of. As far as love is concerned, God has our back. Knowing that God loves us so tenderly and covers everything that concerns us, we can with confidence and assurance love God, ourselves and our neighbors in the depth that God gives to this word.

“you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your strength.’ This is the first commandment.” (Mark 12:30)

This means that you will love God supremely. You will love him with your whole being, independently of the love you have for yourself. If you do not love yourself, too bad. But you will love God in spite of yourself. You will let yourself be consumed in God. No more room for self-love.

The question then is: Do you love God?

The answer, for some, may come from self-righteousness and for others from guilt. Here is the truth: if you are in Christ, you love God. Because God’s love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us (Rom 5:5). Do you understand that? You love God. This supreme love is communicated to you by the Holy Spirit. Moreover, it cannot die out because the Holy Spirit is always in you.

You may be surprised! Someone may even go so far as to say that they do not know God well enough to love him fully. But of course you know him! “We know that the Son of God has come, and has given us an understanding, that we know him who is true, and we are in him who is true, in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life.” (1 John 5:20). That is clear: if you have accepted Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior, it is because you received the revelation of God. So you know God and you love him! Your spirit is so in love with this love that it sings it at every moment. “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”” (Rom 8:15)

Abba! Father! That is what your regenerated spirit sings without ceasing. Do you know what “Abba Father” means? It is: “DADDY, DADDY!” In modern times, children would say: “MY DEAR DADDY!” and if you want to make a long sentence, you would say: “I LOVE YOU, MY DEAR DADDY!”

You know God and you love him. Give in to this deep feeling of your heart. Say it: I LOVE THE LORD MY GOD WITH ALL MY HEART, WITH ALL MY SOUL, WITH ALL MY MIND, AND WITH ALL MY STRENGTH! HE IS MY DADDY AND I LOVE HIM MORE THAN ANYTHING IN THE WORLD!

To express your love for your dear Daddy, sing, dance, bow down, tell him sweet words. The sacred writer says it in other terms: “speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always concerning all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to God, even the Father;” (Eph 5:19-20)

It is obvious that without love for oneself, love for one’s neighbor is either impossible or a useless ordeal. The Lord Jesus Christ says: you shall love your neighbor as yourself. In saying these words, the Lord assumes that every person has love for themselves. “For no man ever hated his own flesh; but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph 5:29)

So, despite all your feelings toward your own person, you love yourself. The Bible says that you love yourself; so it is true: you love yourself. That is why you are careful in your movements, you eat when you are hungry, you shower, you feel sorry for yourself when you suffer, you are uncomfortable with the imperfections in you.

The only problem is that we believe a little too much the negative things that were instilled in us about ourselves. Through insults, contempt and the dramatization of our past mistakes, our parents, guardians and friends have led us to believe wrong things about ourselves. That is why some people have an inferiority complex, believe themselves incapable of certain things, are slaves to fear, blame themselves for almost their whole past, are afraid to commit, hate certain parts of their body and even have a disgust for life.

The solution is to refuse to let what people say determine who you are. You are what your Creator says about you. You are so important to him that, for you alone, God gave his only Son to death. It goes so far that, if necessary, Jesus Christ would sacrifice himself again just for you. You are important and you have incredible capabilities: God made you wonderful (Ps 139:14).

We must recognize that:

  • You have flaws
  • You have weaknesses of character
  • You have regrets

No matter! Accept yourself like that. You are going to work on improving yourself. However, you are going to respect yourself and make others respect you. You are going to defend your interests and take care of yourself (Eccl 2:24, Eccl 7:16-18, Eccl 9:7-10).

In any case, as far as the neighbor is concerned, we do not need to love him very much, just a little, that is, as ourselves, and that is all.

But who is this neighbor? When someone asked our Lord the question, his answer was this:

“Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead. By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side. In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’ Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”” (Luke 10:30-37)

In reality, all the people who passed along this road, the priest, the Levite, the Samaritan, and even the robbers who harmed this man are all his neighbors. But only one truly showed himself to be one. The others thought only of themselves. But the Samaritan thought of the man by putting himself in his place. And our Lord tells us to do as he did.

The neighbor is therefore that person. Her, him. This person who smiles at you, but also the one who despises you, insults you, mistreats you, and so on. The neighbor is everyone you can point your finger at.

He is like you: he has a head, two hands, two feet. He has weaknesses and strengths.

He is also different from you. He is perhaps of another sex, ethnic group, race, social class, culture, religion, political opinion. Perhaps he snores, talks a lot, acts clumsily, and so on.

What if it were you?

Do not answer too quickly. Go and live his past, take his feelings, take his phobias and his fears, take his point of view, his level of information and education, and all the other aspects of his being: YOU WOULD SPEAK AND ACT EXACTLY LIKE HIM. And like him, you would wish to be understood, accepted, advised gently, encouraged, helped, forgiven, loved. DO IT FOR HIM!

“Therefore whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.” (Matt 7:12)

Although love for the neighbor already includes brothers and sisters in Christ, we must still insist on brotherly love and learn to practice it. For this, here are a few practices that the Builder must make a habit of:

Have an important moment each day, or a special day each week, when he prays for brothers and sisters in a practical way. It is not about praying that God would bless them, but about observing their lives enough, identifying prayer needs and interceding for a real change.

From time to time, do something for a brother or sister that brings a qualitative and quantitative change in their life. This good deed must be done to a member of the body of Christ, with priority given to Builders. It is not the same person every time.

Never criticize or slander a brother or sister in front of unbelievers. This is not about denying the truth if the person is guilty of the allegation. But if you cannot find true and justifiable reasons that explain their wrongdoing, it is better to keep silent. We must always give the impression that we believe the best of our brothers and sisters because the Holy Spirit is at work in them.

Always favor gentleness when we have to bring back to order our brothers and sisters who wander. We must avoid throwing words of condemnation at them and keeping them stuck in the past by constantly insisting on what they should have done. Instead, we must help them carry the burden. We must lead them to believe in the possibility of getting back up. We must pray with them for their restoration. If you have the financial and material means and if it is necessary, put them at their disposal for their restoration. There is no question of our losing soldiers because they are wounded.

Favor brothers and sisters in the faith over all other relationships.

We have spoken of necessary things, easier said than done. We need divine help. Fortunately, we have the Holy Spirit. If we prefer his company and show it by our dedication to prayer and meditation, he will strengthen us and equip us to put into practice, with joy, this precious commandment of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Where love is most difficult and most decisive is the home.

For if you manage to love with the 13 characteristics of 1 Corinthians 13 in your shop but not in your bedroom, you have not yet learned to love. You have learned to behave. It is not the same thing.

“A peaceful home is a business that works. A steady father is a natural leader. A fulfilled mother is a builder. The quality of your married life determines the quality of everything else — your productivity, your creativity, your health, your faith. You cannot build outside what you have not built inside.”

1 — LOVE IN THE COUPLE

Marriage is the most demanding covenant you will ever sign — and the most beautiful if it is built on the right foundation. This foundation is not compatibility of characters or the passion of the beginning. It is love as God defines it.

“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it;” (Eph 5:25)

“Husbands, love your wives, and don’t be bitter against them.” (Col 3:19)

The love of 1 Corinthians 13 in the home is concrete. Here is how it translates:

1. Handling disagreement without hurting

Every couple has disagreements. What distinguishes a solid home is not the absence of conflict — it is the way of getting through them. “Love is patient and is kind” (v. 4). Patience in conflict looks like this: I do not interrupt. I do not leave the room slamming the door. I do not bring up past mistakes.

2. The difference between winning an argument and preserving a covenant

You can be right and lose your marriage at the same time. Love “doesn’t seek its own way” (v. 5). Ask yourself this question after every disagreement: did I try to be right, or did I try to find our way back to each other?

3. Communication as a spiritual discipline

Truly listening to your spouse — without preparing your answer while they speak — is a spiritual act. It is honor put into practice. Love “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth” (v. 6). Creating a space for true speech in marriage is building a temple in your house.

4. Intimacy as an act of worship

Your spouse’s body is entrusted to you by God (1 Cor 7:4). Marital intimacy is not an animal need to be satisfied — it is a language of the covenant that God invented. Protecting it, caring for it, respecting it, is honoring God in your marriage.

2 — LOVE IN PARENTING

Raising a child is the most responsible and the most meaningful vocation you can receive. It is not natural — it is supernatural. It requires a wisdom that you alone cannot have.

“Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” (Prov 22:6)

“You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” (Eph 6:4)

Three practical axes for the Builder parent:

Authority without violence. Parental authority is not the right to hit — it is the responsibility to guide. A child who obeys out of fear has not learned to obey. He has learned to be afraid. The authority that forms is the one that explains, that sets clear limits and that stays consistent.

Presence without overprotection. Being present means listening to what your child is really saying — not just the words. It is sitting with him, not just giving to him. But presence does not mean living his life for him. A Builder raises children who know how to face difficulty, not children who never had to face any.

The power of parental declarations. Your words about your child are prophecies. “You are worth nothing” forges one identity. “You are capable, you are blessed, God has a plan for your life” forges another. The father who prays with his children, who lays his hands on their heads and blesses them by the word, builds a wall that the world cannot bring down.

For you who are single. What you learn here does not begin at marriage. It begins now — in your family of origin, with your parents, your brothers, your sisters. The way you treat your mother reveals how you will treat your wife. The way you respect your father shapes the way you will exercise your authority. The home you want tomorrow, you prepare today.

3 — GETTING THROUGH FAMILY CONFLICTS

Conflict in the home is not an anomaly. It is a ground for sanctification. Two free people, with different histories, different wounds, different expectations, living under the same roof — disagreement is inevitable. What is not inevitable is destruction.

“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother …” (Matt 5:23-24)

Three steps to get out of a marital conflict:

Step 1 — Listen to understand, not to answer

While he or she speaks, your only task is to understand what this person is really feeling. No defense. No correction. No counter-argument. Just understand. When you have finished listening, rephrase: “What I hear is that you feel… is that right?” Just one question. Wait for the answer.

Step 2 — Express without accusing

When your turn comes, speak with “I” — not with “you”. “I felt ignored” is different from “You always ignore me”. The first opens a conversation. The second opens a war. Love “is not provoked, takes no account of evil” (v. 5). It starts in the way you word your pain.

Step 3 — Commit to a concrete action

A conversation that ends without a concrete commitment solves nothing. This is not a courtroom — it is a covenant. Before leaving the conversation, ask together a simple question: “What are we going to do differently from now on?” One thing. Concrete. Dated.

On forgiveness. Forgiveness is not a feeling. It is a decision. You do not forgive because you feel love. You forgive because you choose to stop holding this person prisoner for what they did to you. Love “takes no account of evil” (v. 5). That does not mean forgetting. It means no longer using the wound as a weapon.

TO MEDITATE ON THIS WEEK

“If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing.”

1 Corinthians 13:1-2

The Builder you are becoming is not measured first by what he builds outside. He is measured first by what he has built in his home.

objectifs: You love God, and you let yourself be loved by Him — not out of obligation, but by revelation.
You love yourself in a healthy way — you have stopped punishing and belittling yourself.
You love your family concretely — not just in feeling, but in specific actions.
You have identified and begun to correct your deficits of love toward the key people in your life.

qcm.q: What does 1 John 4:8 say about God?
qcm.e: “God is love” (1 John 4:8) and love is of God (1 John 4:7).

qcm.q: According to 1 John 4:19, who loved first?
qcm.e: “We love him, because he first loved us.”

qcm.q: How is God’s love poured out in our hearts, according to Romans 5:5?
c: Through the Holy Spirit who was given to us
qcm.e: If you are in Christ, you love God: this love is communicated to you by the Holy Spirit.

qcm.q: What is the only condition for receiving the promise of John 14:2-3 (Jesus will take us to himself)?
qcm.e: Jesus gave no conditions for coming and then making excuses: the only condition is faith in his love.
Abba, Father: “Daddy, Daddy!”, the affectionate cry of the regenerated spirit.

qcm.q: According to Mark 12:30, how must we love God?
c: With all our heart, with all our soul, with all our mind and with all our strength
qcm.e: It is about loving God supremely, with our whole being.

qcm.q: What does Ephesians 5:29 say about self-love?
c: It does not exist among believers
No one has ever hated his own flesh: he nourishes and cherishes it
It is reserved for the proud
qcm.e: The Bible says you already love yourself: you eat when you are hungry, you take care of yourself.

qcm.q: What should we do about the negative things we were led to believe about ourselves?
c: Refuse to let what people say determine who we are: we are what our Creator says about us
Believe them and get used to them
qcm.e: God made you wonderful (Psalm 139:14); you are precious to him.

qcm.q: Who is the neighbor, according to the parable of the good Samaritan?
c: Anyone, even one who despises us; whoever puts himself in his place shows himself to be a neighbor
qcm.e: Luke 10:30-37: the neighbor is the one you do good to by putting yourself in his place.

qcm.q: What does the question “What if it were you?” invite us to do?
c: Put yourself in the other’s place and act as we would want others to act toward us
qcm.e: Matthew 7:12: whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them.

qcm.q: Among the practices of brotherly love, what must the Builder avoid in front of unbelievers?
c: Believing the best of his brothers
Criticizing or slandering a brother or sister
qcm.e: If you cannot find true and justifiable reasons, it is better to keep silent: the Holy Spirit is at work in them.

qcm.q: What does Ephesians 5:25 ask of husbands?
c: To provide only for her material needs
To love their wives as Christ loved the assembly and gave himself up for it
qcm.e: A foundation of the couple: love as God defines it.

qcm.q: After every disagreement in the couple, what question does the module invite us to ask?
c: Did I try to be right, or to find our way back to each other?
How long will the argument last?
qcm.e: You can be right and lose your marriage at the same time: the point is to preserve the covenant.

qcm.q: What are the three steps to get out of a marital conflict?
c: Listen to understand, express without accusing, commit to a concrete action
qcm.e: Listen to understand, not to answer; speak with “I”; finish with a concrete action.

qcm.q: What does the manual say about forgiveness?
c: It is reserved for serious offenses
It is a decision: we stop holding the other prisoner for what they did
It is a feeling we must wait for
We must forget in order to forgive
qcm.e: You do not forgive because you feel love, but because you choose to set the other free.

exercices.titre: Role play — a conflict at home
exercices.consigne: This exercise is done in pairs: with your partner, your spouse or a trusted person. If you are alone, act out the scene aloud, playing both roles.
exercices.intro_html:
Choose together a common conflict situation in a household:

• Disagreement over managing the month’s money

• Tension over raising a child

• Frustration over a lack of time spent together

First run (2 minutes): react as you would naturally, without thinking about it.

Second run (3 minutes): replay the same scene applying the 3 steps (listen to understand, express without accusing, commit to a concrete action) and the characteristics of love from 1 Corinthians 13.

Then answer in writing:

champs.label: What concretely changed between the first and the second run?
What is the hardest thing you said or did in the first run?
What does this exercise reveal about you in conflicts?

exercices.titre: My week of acts of love
exercices.consigne: For 7 days, perform one concrete act of love each day, from the closest to the furthest: the home first, then friends, brothers and sisters in Christ, the difficult neighbor, the stranger. Not a feeling: an act. It must be deliberate (you choose it consciously), unusual (you do not ordinarily do it) and practical (a service, a word of blessing, a gesture of attention, a moment offered). If the person of the day is not available, swap with another day. Love without action is dead. You can continue the course as soon as you have started.

cibles: My spouse (if I am single: one of my parents)
One of my children (if I have none: a brother or sister)
The family member with whom it is hardest or most distant (the person in my letter)
A close friend or a colleague
A brother or sister in Christ
Someone who bothers me, despises me or with whom I am in tension
A stranger, or a person in need whom I meet along my way
champs.notePlaceholder: The act done, the reaction observed, what I felt while doing it
champs.intro: A different person each day, from the closest to the furthest.

champs.label: At the end of the 7 days: what this week taught me about my ability to love concretely (optional, fill in when you have finished)

exercices.consigne: Choose the person in your family with whom the relationship is the most difficult or the most distant. Write them a real letter, by hand. You do not necessarily send it, but you write it as if they were going to read it. The letter stays with you: you will only summarize the essentials in the sheet.
exercices.intro_html:
This letter must contain:

• What you appreciate in them, without conditions or “buts”.

• What you did wrong to them, without justifying yourself.

• What you want to change concretely in your relationship.
